topics.description: Confidentiality, integrity and availability — the three properties every security control ultimately serves.
topics.notes: Mapping a given control or incident onto the right leg of the triad is a likely question.

topics.description: Authentication establishes who you are; authorization determines what you may do. Authentication always precedes authorization.
topics.notes: A named comparison and among the most commonly confused pairs on this exam.

topics.description: Recording what was done and by whom, completing the AAA triad alongside authentication and authorization.
Granting only the access required for the task, and no more, so a compromise has limited reach.
Layering independent controls so that no single failure exposes the system.
Trusting no request implicitly by network location, and verifying every one instead.
The total set of points where a system can be attacked; hardening is the practice of reducing it.
A vulnerability is a weakness, a threat is what might exploit it, and risk is the likelihood and impact combined.
topics.notes: These three are constantly used loosely in conversation and precisely in exams.

topics.description: Requiring two or more of something you know, have, or are — so a stolen password alone is insufficient.
Passwords are stored as one-way hashes, with a per-user salt so identical passwords do not produce identical hashes.
topics.notes: Hashing is one-way and is not encryption; conflating them is a common error.

topics.description: One authentication event granting access to many systems.
A key pair where the private key stays with the user and the public key is installed on servers — the standard for SSH and stronger than passwords.
Symmetric uses one shared key and is fast; asymmetric uses a key pair and solves key distribution. TLS uses asymmetric to agree a symmetric key.
topics.notes: A named comparison; the reason both exist together in TLS is the insight.

path: encryption at rest vs in transit
topics.description: Protecting stored data versus protecting data moving across a network. They are separate controls and both are needed.
A one-way fixed-length digest used for integrity checking and password storage. It cannot be reversed.
A certificate binds a public key to an identity; a CA vouches for that binding, and trust flows down the chain.
TLS encrypts and authenticates a connection; HTTPS is HTTP carried inside it. SSL is the obsolete predecessor.
Certificates have a validity window; an expired or mismatched certificate produces browser warnings and failed connections.
Encrypting a whole block device, commonly with LUKS on Linux, so that data is unreadable if the hardware is lost or stolen.
Manipulating people rather than technology, and the most common initial access route in practice.
topics.notes: Technical controls do not fully mitigate this; user awareness is the named defence.

topics.description: Malicious software generally, and specifically software that encrypts data and demands payment — the threat that makes tested offline backups a security control.
Exhausting a resource so legitimate users cannot be served; distributed when mounted from many sources.
Intercepting traffic between two parties, the attack TLS and certificate validation exist to prevent.
Guessing credentials exhaustively, or replaying credentials leaked from elsewhere. Rate limiting, lockout and MFA are the defences.
Supplying input that is executed as code or query, SQL injection being the classic. Input validation and parameterised queries are the defence.
Turning limited access into greater access, whether horizontally to a peer account or vertically to root.
Harm caused by someone with legitimate access, whether deliberate or accidental.
Known weaknesses are catalogued with CVE identifiers and scored; timely patching is the primary remediation.
Removing unnecessary software, closing ports, disabling unused accounts, and tightening defaults.
Filtering traffic and dividing networks so a compromise in one segment does not reach the rest.
Systems that detect suspicious activity, and those that additionally block it.
Retaining and reviewing logs, without which an intrusion cannot be detected or reconstructed.
The prepared sequence: prepare, identify, contain, eradicate, recover, and learn.
topics.notes: Containment precedes eradication; acting out of order is a common wrong answer.

topics.description: Controlling physical access, since an attacker at the console can bypass most software controls.
Disabling root login and password authentication, and preferring keys — the standard baseline for an internet-facing host.
Linux mandatory access control: policy confines what a process may do even when file permissions would allow it, so a compromised service is contained.
Checking GPG signatures and published checksums before trusting software, which is what makes a repository or a downloaded image trustworthy.
topics.notes: Applies the hashing primitive to a concrete supply-chain defence.

topics.description: Systematically probing systems and images for known weaknesses, as a routine practice distinct from detecting an intrusion in progress.
Data that identifies a person directly or in combination, attracting legal obligations wherever it is held.
Health information and cardholder data carry their own regimes — HIPAA and PCI-DSS respectively.
Labelling data by sensitivity — public, internal, confidential, restricted — so controls can be applied proportionately.
At rest, in transit, and in use. Each state needs its own protection, and data in use is the hardest.
Discretionary, mandatory, and role-based access control. RBAC is the common organisational choice.
Generating, storing, rotating and revoking keys. Encryption is only as strong as key custody.
Keeping credentials, API keys and tokens out of source code and images, in a purpose-built store.
topics.notes: Committing a secret to Git is a frequent real-world breach cause; rotating it is the only true fix.

topics.description: Obscuring data, removing identifiability irreversibly, or replacing identifiers with reversible tokens. Only anonymization is one-way.
topics.notes: Pseudonymized data is still personal data under GDPR; anonymized data is not.

topics.description: Controls that detect and block sensitive data leaving the organisation.
Keeping data only as long as needed and destroying it verifiably afterwards.
Ordinary deletion unlinks a file without erasing its blocks; secure disposal requires overwriting, cryptographic erasure, or physical destruction.
topics.notes: That rm does not erase data is the key insight here.

topics.description: Unauthorised exposure of protected data, usually carrying a legal duty to notify within a defined window.
Backups inherit the sensitivity of their contents and require the same encryption and access control as the original.
Demonstrably meeting obligations imposed by law, regulation, or contract — with evidence, not merely intent.
topics.notes: Compliance and security overlap but are not the same; a system can be compliant and insecure.

topics.description: Policy states intent, a standard sets the measurable requirement, and a procedure gives the steps.
A control is a safeguard; evidence proves it operated. Audits examine evidence, not assurances.
A formal examination against a standard, internal or by an external assessor.
Identifying risks and deciding whether to mitigate, transfer, accept, or avoid each.
EU regulation governing personal data, with lawful-basis, minimisation, subject-access and erasure requirements, and extraterritorial reach.
US regulation protecting health information.
A contractual card-industry standard for anyone handling payment card data.
topics.notes: Contractual rather than governmental, unlike GDPR and HIPAA.

topics.description: Voluntary attestation and certification frameworks organisations adopt to evidence their security posture.
Data is subject to the laws of where it is stored, which constrains which cloud regions may be used.
Rules requiring data be kept for a minimum period, which can conflict with deletion rights and must be reconciled deliberately.
The justification for processing personal data; consent is only one of several, and must be freely given.
Meeting the obligations of software licences, including open source attribution and source-provision duties.
Fines, contractual loss, mandatory notification, and reputational damage.
